newsitem.title: USA: Dollar edges higher as investors dump German marks.
newsitem.headline: Dollar edges higher as investors dump German marks.

text.p: The dollar ended slightly higher against major currencies as investors continued to sell German marks amid improving prospects for a planned single European currency.
Funds flocked to the British pound, which would remain outside the proposed European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) and the exodus from the mark helped bolster the dollar.

"Everybody is getting out of marks because it looks like EMU is going to go through. The dollar will benefit from mark weakness," said Francois Akl, chief currency dealer at Gulf International Bank in New York.
The dollar late Friday rose to 1.5244 marks from 1.5236 late Thursday and to 110.90 Japanese yen from 110.67.
The British pound rose to $1.5637 from $1.5614. The dollar climbed to 1.2565 Swiss francs from 1.2544, but fell to Canadian $1.3632 from C$1.3678.
The mark typically enjoys broad investment flows because of Germany's traditional status as the strongest economy in Europe and a fiercely anti-inflation central bank.
But EMU would eliminate the mark and the perceived safety of investing in the German currency.

Meanwhile, Italy formally unveiled its 1997 budget, which Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi asserted would meet strict financial conditions for the lira to join EMU, drawing more funds away from the mark.
"As EMU becomes reality, you don't need the mark as a safe haven anymore," said Hillel Waxman, first vice president for foreign exchange and securities at Bank Leumi Trust Co. of New York.
For the second straight session, the dollar's gains were confined to overseas trading hours, with European investors seen unloading marks.
The dollar dipped briefly against the yen during Tokyo trading on a news report that Bank of Japan officials were concerned that Japanese long-term interest rates were too low.
Japanese officials declined to comment and the dollar soon rebounded amid a general view that Japan's economy was too weak to withstand higher interest rates.
"The Japanese economy is still very weak and they have no reason to raise rates," Akl said.
Dealers reported strong dollar buying from Japanese investors as the Japanese fiscal year midpoint nears. That trend should end when the second half begins October 1.
The dollar now stands just below its 1996 high of 111.19 yen, a key technical level which should complicate future dollar gains, dealers said.
Looking ahead, a Saturday meeting in Washington of the finance ministers from the Group of Seven industrialised nations could offer clues about official views on recent currency market trends.
The group, known as the G7, is expected to focus on efforts to stimulate economic growth in Europe, with any statement on currencies likely to show general complacency, dealers said.
"I think everyone will come in very happy with where the dollar is," said Waxman. "From a currency standpoint, the world is looking fine."
